secoes.titulo: Instruments for assessing severity, prognosis, and organ dysfunction in critically ill patients.

secoes.corpo:
A Intensive Care Unit (ICU) is the hospital environment where the most severely ill patients are concentrated, with imminent risk of death and need for continuous monitoring and complex interventions. In this context, the assessment scales are indispensable tools to quantify severity, predict outcomes, guide therapeutic management, and optimize resource allocation.

Unlike scales used in other specialties—which generally focus on a single organ system—ICU scales are often multisystem , reflecting the complex nature of the critically ill patient, who may present simultaneous dysfunctions in multiple organs.

O APACHE II (Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation) is the most well-known severity score worldwide. Applied in the first 24 hours of admission, it uses 12 physiological variables, age, and comorbidities to estimate the risk of hospital mortality. The SOFA (Sequential Organ Failure Assessment) assesses dysfunction of six organ systems daily, and is now the main criterion for defining sepsis according to the Sepsis-3 consensus: an increase of 2 or more points in SOFA, associated with infection, defines the septic condition.

In addition to severity scores, the intensive care nurse uses scales to delirium detection (CAM-ICU), neurological assessment in sedated or intubated patients (FOUR, Glasgow), pain assessment in non-verbal patients (BPS — Behavioral Pain Scale) and severity stratification in respiratory infections (CURB-65).

The systematic application of these scales, integrated with the Nursing Care Systematization (SAE), allows early detection of clinical deterioration, precise communication during multidisciplinary rounds, and objective evaluation of response to therapeutic interventions.

Intensive Care Scales (ICU)

INTENSIVE CARE

Instruments for assessing severity, prognosis, and organ dysfunction in critically ill patients.

Introduction to Intensive Care Scales
A Intensive Care Unit (ICU) is the hospital environment where the most severely ill patients are concentrated, with imminent risk of death and need for continuous monitoring and complex interventions. In this context, the assessment scales are indispensable tools to quantify severity, predict outcomes, guide therapeutic management, and optimize resource allocation.

Unlike scales used in other specialties—which generally focus on a single organ system—ICU scales are often multisystem , reflecting the complex nature of the critically ill patient, who may present simultaneous dysfunctions in multiple organs.

O APACHE II (Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation) is the most well-known severity score worldwide. Applied in the first 24 hours of admission, it uses 12 physiological variables, age, and comorbidities to estimate the risk of hospital mortality. The SOFA (Sequential Organ Failure Assessment) assesses dysfunction of six organ systems daily, and is now the main criterion for defining sepsis according to the Sepsis-3 consensus: an increase of 2 or more points in SOFA, associated with infection, defines the septic condition.

In addition to severity scores, the intensive care nurse uses scales to delirium detection (CAM-ICU), neurological assessment in sedated or intubated patients (FOUR, Glasgow), pain assessment in non-verbal patients (BPS — Behavioral Pain Scale) and severity stratification in respiratory infections (CURB-65).

The systematic application of these scales, integrated with the Nursing Care Systematization (SAE), allows early detection of clinical deterioration, precise communication during multidisciplinary rounds, and objective evaluation of response to therapeutic interventions.

Schalen en Rekenmachines

APACHE II
Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation

Gold standard for severity assessment in the ICU. Uses 12 physiological variables, age, and chronic diseases. Predicts hospital mortality. Score 0-71.

SOFA
Sequential Organ Failure Assessment

Daily assessment of organ dysfunction (6 systems). Defining criterion for sepsis (Δ ≥ 2). Monitors response to treatment. Score 0-24.

CAM-ICU
Confusion Assessment Method for ICU

Detection of delirium in critically ill patients under mechanical ventilation. 4 characteristics: fluctuation, inattention, disorganized thinking, level of consciousness.

BPS
Behavioral Pain Scale

Pain assessment in patients under mechanical ventilation and sedation. Analyzes facial expression, upper limbs, and ventilator adaptation. Score 3-12.

CURB-65
Ernst van pneumonie

Stratifies severity of community-acquired pneumonia. 5 criteria: confusion, urea, respiration, blood pressure, and age ≥ 65. Score 0-5.

Glasgow
Glasgow Coma Scale

Assessment of level of consciousness in the ICU. Complementary to FOUR in intubated patients. Serial neurological monitoring.
